responses.title: Platforms and scale
responses.question: Which platforms and operating envelope should the first qualified release promise?
responses.recommendation: Windows, Apple-silicon macOS, and Linux for the Mango client and GUI, with provider/telemetry support qualified separately. Start with 1–20 nodes and 100 deployments. Use the proposed idle targets of under 1 percent of one CPU core, 150 MiB background-service memory, and 1 KiB/s average control traffic per node as targets to validate, not promises already established. Report the total footprint including Tailscale and the open GUI separately.
responses.context: This makes “lightweight” testable without claiming unlimited scale. A narrower platform set would reduce initial qualification work. Affects PRODUCT-01, NFR-01–04.
responses.choice_label: Narrow the launch platforms or scale; specify below
responses.notes: Windows is the first GUI path and the first listener to master (though of course clients can enter the network for requests from any node, and might have an arbitrary OS. Defer mac and linux nodes for later implementation steps. Performance targets acceptable, though idle periods with no requests and no changes to network configuration should have average traffic of 0 most of the time.

responses.title: Tailscale installation
responses.question: Should Mango require the existing Tailscale client or embed Tailscale?
responses.recommendation: require an installed, authenticated client initially and make setup checks clear in the GUI. Retain embedding as a packaging option to assess after the stack is chosen. `tsnet` is real, but it creates another authenticated device identity and ties the direct embedding path to Go.
responses.context: Embedding could improve first-run convenience, but its lifecycle, device permissions, and footprint need qualification. Neither option removes user authentication. Affects NET-03, PRODUCT-02.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation

responses.title: Public HTTPS
responses.question: Which public exposure path should Mango support, and should it ever enable exposure automatically?
responses.recommendation: exposure is off until the local owner enables it. Support a general HTTPS reverse proxy, with Tailscale Funnel as an optional guided path when its restrictions fit. Creating an inference key never enables public serving by itself. Publish only the inference surface.
responses.context: A Funnel-only choice is simpler but imposes its domain, port, platform, and bandwidth constraints. Affects PUBLIC-01–04.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation

responses.title: Administrative access from peers
responses.question: Does joining the network grant unrestricted settings administration, or should sensitive changes require a fresh master-password unlock?
responses.recommendation: all enrolled nodes may use resources and view shared state; any node may administer the network after a short local master unlock. Require it for key management, enrollment, shared configuration, retention clearing, and update policy. Keep resource protection and process-control permission local to the host regardless of unlock elsewhere.
responses.context: This retains peer equality while limiting what an unattended unlocked GUI or ordinary peer credential can change. Public inference keys never become administrator credentials. Affects AUTH-07, UI setting boundaries.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation

responses.title: Shared changes during partitions
responses.question: Should the network prioritize safe global ordering or accept administrative changes on isolated peers?
responses.recommendation: serialize membership, ordered join IDs, authority changes, and shared configuration commits through a temporary coordinator with fenced authority and a majority of enrolled voting peers. Any node can originate the change. Inference and immediate local resource withdrawal continue without a majority. Model observations remain host-owned.
responses.context: The cost is significant: in a two-node network, both must be online for globally committed writes. An alternative is eventual merging with explicit conflicts and weaker ordering guarantees. Do not hide this tradeoff behind “decentralized.” Affects NET-05, SYNC-03–05, LOG-12. Also determines whether Q06/Q07 can promise authoritative freshness.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes:
This answer may work, but I want to avoid building a large amount of infrastructure around something like this. I don't want giant receipts being saved, and tons of tooling. I don't want all nodes to have to be online for any writes to be permanent, for example. On the other hand, I find it acceptable for configuration changes to be "newest wins" when it's an explicit decision made with the master key. The first thing a newly-joining node or a node that has been offline should do when re-joining is to reconcile its data with the network, grabbing whatever the most up-to-date information is that it can find beginning at the first node. Other nodes won't proactively probe all others all the time to keep an up-to-date internal map of "who is online". Rather, they'll make that probe when a request comes in directly to the nodes that hold that model. If none are found, they'll then perform a full network probe to see if a new node has joined that is serving it, with a cooldown of, say, 10 seconds. It's okay if information gets stale about other nodes so long as it reconciles over time.

Which BTW, another place to put that is requests sent. If they came with a tiny packet of the "network config hash" and its timestamp, that would also allow the node serving the request to say "hey, I think your config is out of date" or to realize "crap, my own config is out of date, I need to request an update from the client who just sent this.

We have one advantage here. Every network belongs to one user. We can assume there are no hostile peers acting maliciously, only machines that may genuinely be out of date.

responses.title: Password recovery and compromise
responses.question: What should recovery preserve, and must the printed recovery record rebuild authority after all peer state is lost?
responses.recommendation: support both password replacement on a surviving network and authority recovery from an adequate offline recovery record. Ordinary recovery rotates the master/recovery authority and invalidates administrative sessions while preserving enrolled nodes and existing inference keys. Offer a separate compromise-recovery action that revokes peers/keys and requires reenrollment. Neither path recovers deleted logs or provider secrets automatically.
responses.context: A full compromise recovery is more disruptive but appropriate when secrets were stolen. Lost-all-peers recovery needs more than a short password-reset code and cannot reconstruct a lost catalog or key registry without a replica/backup. Forced recovery without the old quorum starts a new network generation and prevents old partitions from regaining write authority automatically. Affects AUTH-04–06.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes:
Important that private information in a network like this = log data, which might have sensitive user requests. That's what we should clear. Important authority = issuing new keys.  

Non private information = models, aliases, machines on the network, routed model capabilities, etc. If we do a full reset, we should preserve the latter information while dumping all issued keys and clearing logs. Each machine will likely need to reapply to join, but it could preserve its information about models such that it can start serving them again with the same stored benchmarks once the new master password is registered. It's okay if it's a little disruptive, we expect it to be rare.

responses.title: Revocation while peers are offline
responses.question: How much stale authorization is acceptable, and what happens to work already using a revoked key?
responses.recommendation: public ingress may accept only authoritative revocation state no older than 60 seconds, refreshed on demand during traffic; if freshness cannot be established, fail closed for new public work. Cancel queued and active requests as soon as their serving node learns the revocation, and refresh authority for long-running public work under the same bound. Trusted private peer inference may continue while partitioned, but known revocations always win.
responses.context: This introduces bounded security-related network checks. Immediate worldwide revocation with indefinite offline availability is not achievable. A longer window improves availability but increases exposure. Affects KEY-07/09–11.
responses.notes: Valid keys are stored locally. If a key is revoked, that status is pushed across the network when the revocation is made. If the machine it is pushed to has an older version of the authoritative hashed record, it replaces. If it is pushed to a machine that was offline, when that machine first comes online, it should update its stored keys from another peer before even taking a request (unless there are none, of course). Only if there are no other peers can its record be considered the most up to date (since it has no one to tell it otherwise). This does mean that there are rare cases a revoked key could continue to work on a client that was down intermittently, if the entire rest of the network is down when that client comes back online. That's acceptable. For safety reasons, keys should only be ALLOWED to be issued or revoked unless the network has a known size of 1, OR at least 1 other node is online. (rare conflicts are still possible, and we should try to apply all changes in them where they dont' conflict. For example, creating one key doesn't prevent revoking another. Keys can't be modified once created, so we don't have to worry about modify actions. They're made with a name, permissions, and priority, and those stay forever until revoked.

responses.title: Key policy and limits
responses.question: Should keys have a fixed priority, what additional scopes should exist, and which initial limits are appropriate?
responses.recommendation: one fixed low/normal/high priority per key, default normal; permitted task types plus optional alias restrictions; unique display name; 90-day default expiry with an explicit non-expiring choice for private integrations. Begin with the unknown-key lookup limits in KEY-07 and finite configurable per-key rate, concurrency, and payload limits. Label these limits as per-ingress unless a later network-wide quota design is explicitly required.
responses.context: Trusted peer-originated work carries its node identity and defaults to normal priority; elevation requires administrative policy. Forwarding public traffic never removes its original restrictions. Do not promise a strict global rate quota from independent node counters. The exact workload-dependent valid-key limits can be tuned during qualification. Affects KEY-01–08, QUEUE-08.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes: non-expire is always a choice for any key created if the user wishes. Concurrency and payload limits and for the whole network not per key, we have priority for that. IE: if the user wants to send 10 requests on one key, they can. We don't have to worry about hardening this private service with extra verification infrastructure. Payload limits are set as high as is practical for requests, but most requests will be much lower than the limit in practice.

responses.title: Authority over existing inference servers
responses.question: May Mango shut down an existing server it did not start, and who grants that authority?
responses.recommendation: the local owner explicitly places each provider in managed or attached mode. Managed mode grants a defined load/unload/stop path and is required for a promise of automatic resource reclamation. Attached mode permits inference but clearly states when Mango cannot release the provider's resources. Do not stop unrelated processes or the provider GUI merely because names match.
responses.context: Automatic downloads, provider installation, training, and weight distribution remain outside the initial scope. This qualifies the original blanket shutdown behavior where Mango lacks control. Affects PROVIDER-03–07, RESOURCE-06/07, SCOPE-09.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation

responses.title: Initial API coverage
responses.question: Which exact provider profiles and client protocols must the first complete release support?
responses.recommendation: qualify Unsloth Studio/API and `unsloth run`, LM Studio native management plus inference, and supported llama-server single-model/router profiles. Cover model listing, chat completions with streaming and client-executed tool calls, embeddings, image generation, transcription, speech generation, and a specifically named structured-decision contract. Use the documented System One style as the decision-contract candidate to validate. Support each operation where the installed backend/model provides it.
responses.context: Treat full Responses, Anthropic Messages, video, realtime duplex audio, and general persistent job/file workflows as separately approved extensions. This keeps image/audio/decisions in scope without promising every vendor API. Affects PROVIDER-07, API-01–04.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation
responses.notes: Unsloth and LM studio both give ways to know which models are loaded, and instruct models to be unloaded. These should be used when in managed mode.

responses.title: Provider tools and code execution
responses.question: May an inference request cause a provider to run code, browse, or invoke tools on a contributing host?
responses.recommendation: no provider-side execution by default. Preserve tool calls returned to and executed by the client. Explicitly disable backend-hosted tools when forwarding into a localhost provider, because the backend may otherwise trust the request as local.
responses.context: Allowing host execution would need separate local permission, key scope, isolation, and failure semantics. It should not be smuggled into ordinary text inference. Affects API-05.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation
responses.notes: Only client-executed tools for now in initial release.

responses.title: Alias compatibility beyond modalities
responses.question: Should alias validation remain strictly modality-only, or add technical checks for outputs that must be interchangeable?
responses.recommendation: retain exact matching of input/output modality sets and never validate quality claims. Also require compatible embedding dimensions/encoding and warn that equal dimensions do not establish a common vector space. Pin an embedding collection to a deployment or owner-declared compatible family. Preserve deployment-specific feature and context checks for every request.
responses.context: The embedding rule is an explicit extension to your validation limit; it prevents silent corruption without judging model intelligence. If rejected, record that callers assume all embedding compatibility risk. Affects MODEL-02–06.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation
responses.notes: I want minimal verification infrastructure here. But knowing what kind of output/input are required prevents a request from failing.

responses.title: Benchmark permission and context verification
responses.question: Should full-context tests run automatically even when expensive, and how should unreported limits be handled?
responses.recommendation: get local permission for the benchmark suite, show its expected size, and make it cancelable. Measure short, half, and full usable context with reserved output and synthetic input, subject to a time/resource budget. Mark skipped or failed tests incomplete and schedule conservatively. Require a configured or verified served limit when the provider cannot report one; never silently substitute the model's theoretical maximum.
responses.context: This retains your full-context measurement requirement while allowing an enormous or unsafe test to be deferred honestly. Affects CONTEXT-04, BENCH-01–06.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation
responses.notes: When joining a node selects what to do about benchmarks as "never", "now", and "when convenient." This setting applies to any later models or providers added to that node without another request for consent. Now means that all benchmarks must be finished before that machine serves anything. when convenient automatically tries to add a benchmark whenever there are no client requests to that node (not the whole network!) after a simple 5 minute cooldown, and can be interrupted by any incoming requests.

responses.title: Memory safety defaults
responses.question: Which default safety margins and overlap policy should apply before a node is fully characterized?
responses.recommendation: reserve the greater of 15 percent or 2 GiB host/unified memory and the greater of 10 percent or 1 GiB per discrete GPU, adjustable locally. Use conservative non-overlap for unmeasured combinations. Require context/concurrency peak evidence and a live admission check before overlapping models.
responses.context: These are starting values to calibrate, not universal guarantees. A provider can still allocate unexpectedly, and another local program can race for memory. Affects MEMORY-01–06, BENCH-06.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes: 15 percent with a min of 2gb and a max of 5gb host RAM by default. 1gb host VRAM by default (this number doesn't scale, it's flat). It can be set as low as 0mb, which will require the user accept a warning that it may cause system instability or shutdown if they set the number lower than the default. However, we honor the user's choice once they consent. (and they don't have to consent again once they do so on that node).

responses.title: Activity detection and cooldown
responses.question: What should trigger withdrawal, when should contribution resume, and what happens when process attribution is unavailable?
responses.recommendation: local CPU/GPU/memory observation with up to 2-second samples, a 10-second sustained external-load trigger, immediate withdrawal for severe memory pressure, and five continuous quiet minutes before resuming. Renew the quiet period on new load. Manual leech mode persists. Treat missing attribution as a visible limitation and require a conservative local choice before automatic contribution.
responses.context: The provisional external-load threshold needs hardware calibration; detecting “any input” should not automatically mean heavy load. Affects RESOURCE-02–07.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation
responses.notes: 2 seconds seems like the maximum frequency, we don't want to hit the machine with constant polling. Can be set lower per machine. Also we should let the user set cutoff percentages and cooldown time, per node. memory pressure cause instant cooldown.(which we log, since this seems like an obvious point of failure if we start shutting down on our own induced loads)

responses.title: Scope of queue purging
responses.question: Should a higher-priority arrival clear every lower-priority queued request on that node, or only requests competing for the same resources?
responses.recommendation: clear only conflicting lower-priority work. A job using an independent GPU or genuinely nonconflicting CPU capacity should continue or be admitted if it cannot delay the higher-priority reservation.
responses.context: This is a deliberate narrowing of “all lower priority requests in the queue.” Literal node-wide purging is simpler to describe but can reject useful work without freeing the needed resource. Affects QUEUE-05/06.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation

responses.title: Scarcity versus priority
responses.question: Does a low-priority request with one possible destination outrank a high-priority request with several destinations?
responses.recommendation: no. Keep safety, authorization, and the explicit priority admission/rejection rules hard. Route flexible work elsewhere to maximize service, then use fewer eligible destinations to break contention among equal-priority requests, followed by FIFO.
responses.context: Your “always lower priority” scarcity sentence and the later priority hierarchy conflict in this case. If scarcity should override key priority, say so explicitly; the queue rejection rules will need corresponding changes. Affects PRODUCT-05, ROUTE-02/03.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes: Yes, it does. If we can route a high priority request to another machine on its next request, then we can serve more requests at once with our network resources. This does not interrupt an ongoing request, it just allows the lower priority request to queue when it otherwise would not)

responses.title: Active work and starvation
responses.question: Should ordinary priority changes abort running inference, and how should a waiting large model avoid endless postponement by small requests?
responses.recommendation: let active requests finish during ordinary scheduling. Higher priority displaces queued work, while local activity, explicit cancellation, revocation, and faults can abort active work. Reserve an admitted scarce request's next feasible start and stop backfilling jobs that would delay it. Permit safe cancellation of loading work before inference begins when justified.
responses.context: Retain strict priority rather than silently aging low-priority work upward; under sustained high load, low-priority work may starve or be rejected. Affects QUEUE-07, ROUTE-06, MOVE-01.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation

responses.title: Client identity and affinity
responses.question: How should Mango identify a continuing conversation, how long should it remember it, and how long may cache reuse delay a request?
responses.recommendation: use an explicit session identifier scoped to authenticated key identity, with bounded in-memory prefix comparison/digests as fallback. Expire ordinary affinity five minutes after completion. Keep unrelated work under the same key independent. Wait for a cached instance only when estimated benefit beats another placement and the client deadline permits it.
responses.context: Never equate source IP or API key with one conversation. Do not persist prompt bodies solely for affinity. Affects AFFINITY-01–05; the future `best` five-minute rule is already confirmed.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation
responses.notes: we want to also store client true identity (IP) as part of either logging option. We will use this for later QOS provisioning.

responses.title: Retries and partial results
responses.question: May Mango automatically restart a request elsewhere after execution starts or the client has received output?
responses.recommendation: automatic retry only when no output has been committed and the operation is known to be replay-safe. After partial output or possible side effects, return an interruption with request/attempt identity. Require an explicit client retry rather than concatenating a second generation into the original stream.
responses.context: Reassigning queued work remains allowed after ownership transfer. Live cache or backend-held conversation migration is not promised. Affects QUEUE-03, MOVE-03–05.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes: Not after execution starts unless the running execution fails first. Once a client gets the output, no. There's no point, they already got their output, even if that output was an error. Though we should prefer retrying if another node can be found rather than sending the error to client.

responses.title: Queue limits and overload
responses.question: What bounds and failure contract should apply when work cannot start promptly?
responses.recommendation: start with 64 waiting requests per serving node, 8 per key per node, and 120 seconds of queue residence for ordinary text/embedding work, plus finite byte limits and separate media deadlines. Use 429 for a client's rate/quota limit and 503 for unavailable inference capacity, with clear reason codes and useful retry hints. Bound rerouting attempts by distinct candidates and the request deadline.
responses.context: Long-running media may need larger explicit deadlines; no request should wait indefinitely. These counts are tuning defaults, not a substitute for byte/resource limits. Affects QUEUE-08–10, ROUTE-07.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes: 120 of queue residence rejected, configurable master network setting default to 5 minutes. Local inference can be slow. Limits should be set generously for the maximum plausible request given context size, not strictly. Remember: clients are not hostile.

responses.title: Low traffic and failure detection
responses.question: Is a small amount of bounded liveness and local inventory checking acceptable when event APIs are insufficient?
responses.recommendation: yes. Prefer events, cached state, demand-driven checks, and daily reconciliation. Allow a slow local provider fallback, initially no more often than once a minute while enabled, and cheap bounded checks for active routing, security freshness, and temporary coordination. Do not scan every peer per request or fetch unchanged full catalogs repeatedly.
responses.context: Without these exceptions, an externally changed server or dead peer can remain stale until the next request or daily refresh. Event API support also differs by provider/version. Affects SYNC-06, NFR-03, NET-03, KEY-09.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes: Per hour, not per minute when the network is idle. Once per day every node should attempt to reconcile even if not enabled. Ongoing requests carry signals about node integrity that can prompt more frequent updates, but this should be because a hash. is passed with a request and that hash shows the local node is stale, not because a request prompted a general update with no staleness signal. Genuine coordination such as for adding nodes, changing settings, and routing real current requests is of course exempt from this limitation.

responses.title: GUI form and headless machines
responses.question: Should the product support headless machines, and what form should the GUI take?
responses.recommendation: a desktop/tray experience backed by a service, with an authenticated local browser GUI usable for headless deployments. Keep the layout responsive and accessible, and allow shared model administration from any enrolled node. Resource-protection settings still require local host access.
responses.context: Do not add a native mobile app or publicly exposed admin console to the initial scope. The exact UI technology belongs in the later plan. Affects UI-01–08.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes: Generally yes, though I don't want us jumping through expensive accessibility hoops. It's a pretty basic app. Anything we can cheaply provide without tons of verification is fine.

responses.title: Logging contents and privacy
responses.question: Should sparse logging be the default, what does verbose “exactly” include, and does `tts` mean tokens per second?
responses.recommendation: default sparse; interpret `tts` as tokens per second and name it explicitly. Verbose records exact inference request bodies with explicit credential exclusions; do not retain response bodies by default. Off creates no persistent request logs, including a hidden per-request audit trail. Required revocation/configuration/update state remains operational state, not logging.
responses.context: If full responses are wanted, add them explicitly with retention and storage implications. Prompt text can contain secrets even after transport credentials are removed. Affects LOG-01–09.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes: yes, tts appears to be a typo for tps. Verbose excludes credential tokens but DOES record the token identifier name AND also records responses. That's the point of verbose. Input and output are recorded. Operational state changes can have their own logging that will be useful during development and can be disabled. We can also subdivide verbose into "Everything" which includes response bodies and Verbose which excludes them.

responses.title: Daily logs and deletion
responses.question: Which day boundary, retention, completeness, and clearing behavior should apply across intermittently connected nodes?
responses.recommendation: one network timezone selected at setup, defaulting to the first node's timezone; UTC timestamps; seven days of raw records and thirty days of aggregate metadata, within a 1 GiB per-node total cap. The lowest eligible join ID collects; offline peers produce a visibly incomplete aggregate, with late merge and deduplication. Network clear remains pending for offline peers and applies a deletion generation before their old data can rejoin.
responses.context: This does not guarantee archival redundancy or deletion of user exports. Affects LOG-10–18.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation
responses.notes: generally agree, but an incomplete log should still be provided when requested. A log that's missing pieces is better than a log that has nothing.

responses.title: Coordinated updates
responses.question: Does “at the same time” mean coordinated queueing or simultaneous restart, and how much can a node update automatically?
responses.recommendation: coordinate one verified release intent and queueing window, then perform rolling installation with bounded draining, local deferral, health verification, and rollback when the data format permits it. Warn before proceeding when a peer cannot verify eligibility; require the initiating user's explicit compatibility-risk override. Never override an invalid signature.
responses.context: Coordinate Mango only. Leave Tailscale, drivers, providers, and model weights under their own update controls. Simultaneous restarts would deliberately remove all capacity and complicate recovery. Affects UPDATE-01–04/08–11.
responses.choice_label: Accept the full recommendation
responses.notes: This feature won't even work since we won't have an update server yet, we'll just make sure it has plumbing for when that server does exist.

responses.title: Mixed-version compatibility
responses.question: How much backward compatibility should releases promise without requiring all nodes to match?
responses.recommendation: publish a feature/protocol compatibility matrix and initially support the current and previous compatible protocol generation. Negotiate shared features regardless of application version numbers. Keep diagnostic connectivity where possible, but reject specifically incompatible operations safely.
responses.context: “Do not lock out different versions automatically” cannot mean decoding unknown or unsafe protocols. Affects UPDATE-05–07.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes: I don't want lots of verification overhead. We instead provide "Cutoffs" in a release that disqualify all older releases when they are made but allow any newer releases that don't themselves come after another cutoff. Other releases that don't include one of these cutoff flags are permitted until the next cutoff flag, creating windows where "we can change somethings so long as the protocol doesn't change." When the protocol genuinely changes, we create a cutoff, bounding into a group of products with compatible communication protocols.

responses.title: Best-model interpretation and preparation
responses.question: Are the proposed capability ratings, capacity tiers, classifier fallback, and reserved name appropriate for the future feature?
responses.recommendation: shared labels and deployment-specific 0–5 ratings with unrated distinct from zero; one primary task label; first choose the strongest eligible open-capacity deployment, including safe immediate cold loading; then prefer eligible loaded deployments that can legally queue; then the best other legal queue. Keep five-minute related-request affinity. Use one explicitly configured decision deployment, bounded classification, and an owner-chosen fallback or clear error if it is unavailable. Reserve `best` now, but do not run this feature yet.
responses.context: This resolves the otherwise ambiguous loaded-but-no-capacity fallback and keeps classification from becoming recursive. It does not judge user model ratings. Affects MODEL-05, BEST-01–12.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes: The thing I don't like is the "one primary task label" models may have a score at code, creative writing, formal writing, summary generation--arbitrary user tasks. Where models can have competency in all those tasks at different scores.  Incoming REQUESTS must be rated to only whatever ketyword in the system best matches the available options, only one keyword per request.

responses.title: Queue survival after crashes
responses.question: Should queued inference survive a Mango restart and execute later automatically?
responses.recommendation: no durable inference queue initially. Keep bounded queues in memory, fail outstanding client connections clearly on restart, and require client retry under the replay policy. Persist configuration and required security/update state, not a hidden backlog of prompts.
responses.context: Durable media jobs may later require a separate explicit contract with result retrieval, cancellation, retention, and duplicate-execution protection. Affects QUEUE-08, API-04, MOVE-05.
responses.choice_label: My own answer / modify the recommendation
responses.notes: If client disconnects or is interrupted, the request can fail with no resume. What I want to be a little more durable is if the network has a failure. Since the client is still listening to whatever node it talked to, that node can check to see if another node can serve the request before failing that client. That's what I mean by durable. If the answer is still no, that client can still fail. Otherwise, the network can retry somewhere else. If the disconnect is on the client side, no retry guarantee is provided or expected. We should even try to forward the cancelation to the destination when a client is no longer listening, that way we don't waste resources for a client who isn't there.

# Mango product scope

Mango shares inference capacity across the user's machines without requiring a particular inference engine or a common local network. It routes whole requests to existing servers, protects each machine's local workload, and exposes a consistent catalog and access policy.

## Product requirements

**PRODUCT-01 — C.** Support any number of installed peers as a product concept. Each peer can access inference resources across the enrolled Mango network. The supported and tested scale must be stated explicitly; the product cannot promise unlimited capacity or cost-free replication.

**PRODUCT-02 — C.** Make Tailscale the network foundation from the beginning. Machines may be on different physical networks. Users authenticate with Tailscale and separately enroll into the intended Mango network.

**PRODUCT-03 — C.** Make nodes lightweight, favor pushed changes and demand-driven requests, and avoid constant network polling. A contributor may become a leech manually or automatically when other activity needs its resources.

**PRODUCT-04 — C.** Connect to Unsloth, LM Studio, and llama.cpp out of the gate. Keep additional providers and inference protocols extensible. Text, image, audio, embeddings, and structured decisions belong in the product scope; exact first-release contracts are pending Q10.

**PRODUCT-05 — C.** Prefer serving as many requests as possible with the available nodes, then request priority, then first in first out. Preserve the explicit low-priority rejection and queue eviction rules. Resolve their interaction with model scarcity in Q16–Q18 rather than silently replacing them with a conventional scheduler.

**PRODUCT-06 — C.** Provide a responsive GUI on every machine. It can configure shared model endpoints, aliases, capabilities, and ratings across the network. Resource protection settings remain local to the machine they protect.

**PRODUCT-07 — C.** Support scoped, individually revocable inference keys; optional internet HTTPS serving; coordinated software updates; configurable logging; and daily or on-demand network log aggregation.

**PRODUCT-08 — F.** Reserve the future `best` routing feature described in its own document. Its model-selection logic is not part of the initial implementation.

## Terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Mango network | An application trust group with its own identity and credentials; it is not automatically the whole tailnet. |
| Peer or node | One enrolled Mango installation, identified independently of hostname and IP address. |
| Join ID | A persistent, ordered enrollment identifier. Its order determines the oldest eligible log collector. It is not a routing priority. |
| Contributor | A node allowed to accept inference work on its local resources. |
| Leech | A node that may submit and route requests but contributes no inference compute. |
| Ingress node | The Mango node a client connects to. It retains the client connection and routes work. |
| Serving node | The node that admits a request to its execution queue and controls the local provider. |
| Provider | An existing inference server and its management interface, such as LM Studio. |
| Model artifact | A particular set of weights, quantization, tokenizer, and associated files. |
| Model instance | A model loaded with a particular context, device allocation, runtime, and concurrency configuration. |
| Model alias | The client-visible name that may group compatible deployments, even of different quality or quantization. |
| Capability | A user-defined task label such as coding, writing, or classification. This differs from a technical feature such as image input or tool-call output. |
| Rating | A user assessment of a deployment's strength at one capability; it is not a verified benchmark score. |
| Modality | A type of input or output, such as text, image, audio, or embedding vectors. |
| Eligible destination | A contributor satisfying the request's authorization, protocol, modalities, context, and resource requirements. |
| Open capacity | Capacity available to admit execution now within safety limits, including the chosen policy for loading an unloaded model. It does not mean merely that a model is installed. |
| Affinity | A preference to return related requests to the same provider instance to reuse its cache or state. |
| Queue | Work admitted to wait at a serving node. An ingress forwarding record is not a second execution queue. |

## Settled interpretations

**SCOPE-01 — I.** The network distributes independent requests. It does not combine GPU memory across machines, split one model across the WAN, or transfer live model execution between unlike runtimes. A backend may itself use multiple local GPUs; Mango treats that as one serving deployment.

**SCOPE-02 — I.** Peer equality does not require a permanently running central inference server. The first node initializes the network; it need not stay alive to route inference. A temporary coordination role for shared metadata or logs does not grant ownership of other nodes' local controls.

**SCOPE-03 — I.** Tailnet membership alone does not grant Mango membership. Conversely, Mango enrollment does not bypass Tailscale policy or expose unrelated services on another machine.

**SCOPE-04 — I.** A leech still receives client requests, control messages, and catalog updates. It must remain usable as an ingress and as a GUI. Shutting down inference does not mean shutting down Mango or Tailscale.

**SCOPE-05 — I.** Model availability has several states: installed but not loaded; loading; loaded and available; loaded and busy; unloading; disabled; unreachable; and failed. A stale advertisement is a routing hint, not permission to exceed the serving node's current resources.

**SCOPE-06 — I.** Aliases do not certify model quality, identical tokenization, identical embeddings, or shared caches. GGUF and MLX deployments can share a name while retaining separate measurements and provider identities.

**SCOPE-07 — I.** Resource-driven relocation usually changes where queued work or the next request runs. Completing an active request before unloading, as in the supplied example, is distinct from aborting it because local user activity takes precedence.

**SCOPE-08 — I.** The inference network is private infrastructure controlled by trusted owners. Scoped public clients are outside that administrative trust group. Protecting against a fully compromised peer requires removing it and rotating affected authority; a peer that serves a request necessarily sees that request's contents.

## Scope boundaries

**SCOPE-09 — P, Q09/Q10.** Integrate installed providers and models first. Do not add a model marketplace, training, automatic weight downloads, weight distribution, billing, or a general remote shell. Starting or stopping an explicitly managed provider is within scope. Future protocol adapters must not turn ordinary inference access into arbitrary host administration.

**SCOPE-10 — I.** Publishing a public inference endpoint is optional and separate from creating a key. A key does not create a DNS name, issue a TLS certificate, open a firewall, or configure a public proxy.

**SCOPE-11 — I.** Requirements may later be implemented in stages. No stage order, sprint breakdown, technology selection, or implementation estimate is approved by this draft.

## Proposed measurable targets

**NFR-01 — P, Q01.** Initially qualify Windows, macOS on Apple silicon, and Linux for the Mango client and GUI; qualify provider and telemetry combinations individually. Test 1–20 peers and 100 advertised deployments. Larger networks may work but are outside the first measured envelope.

**NFR-02 — P, Q01.** With 20 peers, no inference, GUI closed, and an unchanged catalog: target less than 1 percent of one CPU core averaged over 15 minutes and at most 150 MiB resident memory for Mango's background service. Measure the GUI, Tailscale, providers, and optional embedded networking separately and also report the total installed idle footprint. Do not hide a bundled dependency's cost.

**NFR-03 — P, Q01/Q22.** Target no recurring full catalog fetches other than the daily reconciliation. Target at most 1 KiB/s average idle Mango control traffic per node at the stated scale, excluding inference and one-time reconciliation bursts. Instrument message counts, bytes, wakeups, reconnects, and CPU so these claims can be checked.

**NFR-04 — P, Q01.** Target local GUI feedback within 200 ms for ordinary actions; show progress for network-dependent operations. Target less than 25 ms p95 Mango admission and routing overhead on a local healthy path, excluding authorization refresh, provider work, model loading, queue time, and WAN transit. Report these exclusions with measurements.

**NFR-05 — I.** Bound queues, connection buffers, cached request state, pending synchronization, unknown-key lookups, and logs. Saturation must produce a defined failure rather than unbounded RAM use or silent data loss.

**NFR-06 — I.** Timing claims must be measured on named hardware and scenarios. Reachability, revocation, and metadata freshness guarantees must name their behavior under sleep, packet loss, partitions, and clock changes.

# Mango network and security requirements

Tailscale supplies private connectivity. Mango supplies enrollment, resource access, model metadata, and inference-key authority. These are separate trust boundaries, including when all devices belong to the same person.

## Connectivity and joining

**NET-01 — C.** A newly started node actively discovers reachable Mango peers through its tailnet and negotiates enrollment. It prompts for the master password when joining an existing network. An already enrolled node reconnects with its own identity rather than asking for the master password after every boot.

**NET-02 — I.** A peer must retain a small inbound service for enrollment handshakes, authenticated control messages, and inference traffic. Active discovery removes repeated scans by existing peers; it cannot eliminate listeners needed to receive requests. The requirement is low idle cost, not absence of listening sockets.

**NET-03 — P, Q02/Q22.** Use the installed and authenticated Tailscale client initially. Read the known peer set, try remembered Mango peers first, then probe only candidate tailnet addresses on the Mango service port with bounded concurrency and a deadline. Do not scan the tailnet address range or unrelated ports. Support a manual peer address when enumeration or discovery is restricted. A failed search must not silently create a second network.

**NET-04 — I.** Discovery reveals only enough information to identify a candidate network and negotiate supported versions. A node must authenticate the selected network before disclosing secrets or accepting configuration. Joining an unintended network with the same display name must not be possible solely because its response arrived first.

**NET-05 — P, Q05.** Display a network fingerprint or authenticated invitation and verify it during first enrollment. Assign a persistent node identity and ordered join ID through serialized enrollment. Concurrent enrollments must receive unique ordering; restoring a known node retains its identity only when it proves possession of that identity. Copying an installation must not create two live nodes with the same identity.

**NET-06 — C.** Peer traffic must work across the internet without requiring LAN discovery. Handle direct and relayed Tailscale paths. Do not assume low latency, unlimited bandwidth, synchronized uptime, or a permanent public IP.

**NET-07 — I.** Tailscale logout, expired device authorization, policy changes, or unavailable networking must produce a visible diagnosis. Local inference may continue if otherwise authorized and safe. Such a node must not claim successful network replication.

## Index and synchronization

**SYNC-01 — C.** Maintain a local network index. Push updates when model availability changes and reconcile once daily. A node may request an immediate refresh, including on join. Use deltas and revision summaries where possible rather than routinely transferring the complete catalog.

**SYNC-02 — I.** Propagate enrollment and removal, model registration and removal, aliases and capabilities, effective serving limits, contributor state, key issuance and revocation, logging policy, and update coordination. Dynamic queue and capacity hints may travel with admission responses or material state changes; per-token broadcasts are unnecessary.

**SYNC-03 — I.** Replicated changes require an authenticated origin, identity, revision, and replay protection. Duplicate or out-of-order delivery must be harmless. Deletions and revocations must not be undone by an old snapshot. Fetch a full snapshot only when missing history or a revision mismatch requires it.

**SYNC-04 — P, Q05.** Serialize shared configuration and membership changes through a temporary peer coordinator with a fenced leadership term and a majority of enrolled voting peers. Any node can originate an authorized change. Existing inference can continue on reachable nodes when a majority is unavailable, but globally ordered changes cannot be reported as committed. One-node networks work; a two-node network needs both online for such writes. This is a proposal with a real availability cost, not an implied requirement for inference routing.

**SYNC-05 — I.** Model observations and local resource withdrawal remain owned by the reporting machine and take effect there immediately, including without a majority. Shared requested configuration and locally observed operational state must be distinguishable. A remote edit cannot overwrite a newer local safety state.

**SYNC-06 — P, Q22.** Use available transport and provider events, request-triggered checks, reconnect synchronization, and jittered daily reconciliation. Permit inexpensive bounded liveness checks when necessary for active routes, coordination, or revocation freshness. Permit a slow local provider inventory fallback if no event interface exists. Their limits must be visible and measured; there is no full-network polling loop.

**SYNC-07 — I.** Failed updates enter a bounded retry path with backoff. Mark a peer's state stale when freshness is unknown. On reconnection, reconcile revocations and deletion markers before advertising that stale local information is current. Do not broadcast a separate full network snapshot in response to each peer's daily refresh.

## Network authority and recovery

**AUTH-01 — C.** The first peer establishes a master password and a separate recovery key. The recovery key can replace a lost master password. Show an exportable, printable recovery record and explain that it should be stored outside the network. Never print or upload it automatically.

**AUTH-02 — C.** A user holding the master password can create inference keys from any node. Joining peers requires that authority as well. Ordinary inference must not require sending the master password with every request.

**AUTH-03 — I.** Keep Tailscale credentials, Mango node identities, master/recovery authority, public inference keys, and provider API tokens separate. Never use the master password as an inference bearer token or a transport key. Never store it in plaintext or copy it into logs, URLs, provider requests, or command-line diagnostics.

**AUTH-04 — P, Q04/Q06.** Use the password to unlock administrative authority locally through vetted cryptographic mechanisms; peers ordinarily retain verification material and their own identities. Use a memory-hard password derivation and platform secret storage where available. The actual enrollment and recovery protocol requires security review before implementation; this document does not specify a new cryptographic protocol.

**AUTH-05 — P, Q06.** Recovery advances an authority generation, sets a new master password, rotates the recovery secret, and invalidates administrative sessions and old key-issuing authority. Preserve enrolled node identities and existing inference keys by default, with a distinct compromise-recovery option to revoke and reenroll them. Old backups must not restore superseded authority. Recovery without any surviving trusted state requires the printed record to carry sufficient network recovery material; a password-reset code alone is insufficient.

Forced recovery after loss of the coordination quorum is a disaster-recovery operation into a new network generation. An old partition must not regain write authority automatically. The recovery record restores only the authority it actually contains; it cannot reconstruct the catalog, issued-key registry, logs, or provider secrets without a surviving replica or backup. Reenrollment and key reissuance may therefore be necessary.

**AUTH-06 — I.** Losing both administrative secrets does not erase installed provider models. Existing enrolled peers may still function while their credentials remain usable, but Mango must not offer an unauthenticated takeover path. Creating a replacement network remains possible; imported configuration must not import obsolete authority as valid.

**AUTH-07 — P, Q04.** All enrolled nodes can use resources and view shared state. Require a short administrative unlock for changing shared settings, enrollment, key management, retention deletion, or network update policy. Local-only controls require a session on the target machine. Public inference credentials never grant administrative authority.

## Inference keys

**KEY-01 — C.** Each key has a unique non-private display name for attribution, a stable identifier, allowed inference types, and one of three priority levels. Keys are independently revocable. Creation on any authorized node pushes its verification record to peers.

**KEY-02 — P, Q08.** Give each key one fixed priority: low, normal, or high. Omitted priority is normal. Clients cannot raise priority with a request field. Support optional alias restrictions in addition to task-type scopes, and expiry, rate, concurrent-request, and payload limits. A model name change must not silently broaden an alias-restricted key.

Trusted peer-originated requests carry an authenticated node identity and default to normal priority; elevation requires an administrative policy. A public request forwarded by a peer retains its original key's restrictions and cannot become unrestricted private traffic. Proposed key lifetime is 90 days by default, with an explicit non-expiring choice for private integrations. Limits enforced independently at each ingress must be labeled per-ingress, not represented as strict global quotas.

**KEY-03 — I.** Verify credentials at ingress and enforce their effective authority at the serving node. A forwarded request carries authenticated client/key identity and effective scope and priority; a client-supplied header is not evidence. Do not send Mango credentials to a provider that uses its own credential.

**KEY-04 — I.** Replicate a verification record, not reusable bearer secrets. Show a newly issued secret once; provide replacement and revocation instead of secret recovery. Store token verification material appropriate to high-entropy tokens. A human password's slow verification function must not be run for every random internet token.

**KEY-05 — C.** If a presented key is unknown locally, query other peers sequentially. Stop when a valid authoritative record is found, cache it, and accept only after checking the presented secret, scope, expiry, and revocation state. An individual peer's assertion of validity is insufficient without verifiable authority.

**KEY-06 — I.** Distinguish unknown ID from known ID with an incorrect secret, known revocation, expiry, or insufficient scope. Only the genuinely unknown case triggers discovery. Never let a late valid record override a newer revocation. Peer lookups do not recursively fan out.

**KEY-07 — P, Q07/Q08.** Bound unknown-key recovery by source, ingress-wide budget, concurrent work, number of contacted peers, and total elapsed time. Coalesce identical lookups and maintain a bounded short-lived negative cache. Suggested starting limits are 5 misses/minute/source with burst 5, 30/minute/ingress with burst 10, 2 simultaneous peer lookups, at most 3 peers and 2 seconds per miss, and a 30-second negative cache capped at 1,000 entries. These are tuning proposals. Correctness and known-key inference must survive sustained random IDs and source rotation.

**KEY-08 — I.** Minimize unauthenticated work before parsing or buffering large bodies. Bound uploads, generation limits, connections, queues, compressed expansion, media decoding, and slow clients. Protect outbound media fetches from accessing unintended local or tailnet services. Authentication errors must not reveal the peer inventory or whether a specific secret nearly matched.

**KEY-09 — P, Q07.** Give internet key acceptance a maximum 60-second revocation-state age, refreshed on demand during use. If the node cannot obtain sufficiently current authoritative state, reject new public requests as temporarily unavailable. A cached response from another stale peer cannot extend freshness. Revocation freshness must be tied to committed authority, not merely the time of the last successful peer connection. Trusted private inference may continue under its separately approved policy.

**KEY-10 — I.** No partitioned design can both guarantee immediate global revocation and accept cached authority indefinitely. The UI must show pending propagation and unreachable nodes. A local known revocation takes effect immediately and cannot be overridden by an offline permissive mode.

**KEY-11 — P, Q07.** On revocation, cancel queued requests for that key immediately and cancel active requests when the revocation reaches the serving node. Recheck authority before starting queued work. Authorization freshness for long-running public work must follow the agreed policy rather than being assumed permanent after admission.

## Optional public HTTPS

**PUBLIC-01 — C.** A node can expose authorized inference over public HTTPS when the user enables it. A public client need not join the tailnet or install Mango. Other peers remain privately reachable through the ingress.

**PUBLIC-02 — I.** Public exposure must include valid TLS, request authentication, rate and resource limits, and streaming support. Keep enrollment, provider administration, GUI control, logs, and update commands outside the public inference surface. Do not publish native provider ports as a shortcut around Mango authorization.

**PUBLIC-03 — P, Q03.** Support an existing HTTPS reverse proxy as the general path; offer Tailscale Funnel as a convenience where its domain, port, platform, and bandwidth restrictions fit. Exposing a service remains an explicit local action. The GUI checks the endpoint and explains who can reach it.

**PUBLIC-04 — I.** Trust proxy identity headers only from configured proxies. Apply effective limits even if the external source address is unavailable. A proxy or node changing addresses must not erase the identity used for per-key accounting.

Local browser access also needs authentication and origin/request protections. Being bound to loopback does not make a request from an unrelated web page an authorized local administrator or unrestricted inference client.

# Mango provider and model requirements

Mango routes requests through existing serving infrastructure. Each adapter must describe what its particular server can actually do, including lifecycle control and limits. Sharing an HTTP request format does not make management interfaces interchangeable.

## Provider integration

**PROVIDER-01 — C.** Ship support for Unsloth, LM Studio, and llama.cpp. Additional providers must be addable without changing the scheduler's fundamental rules. Version-specific capabilities must be explicit and testable.

**PROVIDER-02 — I.** An adapter needs operations or explicit unsupported results for: endpoint discovery; authentication; model inventory; loaded instances; effective limits; request execution and streaming; cancellation; loading and unloading; process shutdown; concurrency; health; and resource observations. Not every provider must implement every optional operation, but the GUI and scheduler must not assume it does.

**PROVIDER-03 — P, Q09.** Distinguish managed providers, for which the local owner grants Mango lifecycle authority, from attached providers, for which Mango can only use an existing endpoint. Automatic resource reclamation requires managed authority and a demonstrated release path. An attached server with no unload/stop permission cannot be presented as fully reclaimable.

**PROVIDER-04 — I.** Only the host of a provider executes its local process controls. Identify processes by durable ownership evidence rather than killing all processes with a matching name. Never terminate an unrelated server, provider GUI, training task, or user session to reclaim inference memory. Detect when another controller changes the same server and refresh state.

**PROVIDER-05 — C.** Support endpoint and model configuration from any authorized node's GUI. The owning node validates and applies the change. Changes needing local credentials, new executable access, or expanded shutdown authority must be completed locally, consistent with local resource-control ownership.

**PROVIDER-06 — I.** Discover only configured or recognized local endpoints and user-added endpoints within the approved boundary. Do not run arbitrary URLs, shell commands, or adapter code supplied by an inference client. Store provider tokens on the owning node; shared configuration can show a credential reference and validity state, not the secret.

**PROVIDER-07 — P, Q10.** Qualify Unsloth Studio/API and the `unsloth run` serving profile explicitly, LM Studio's native management API plus inference API, and supported llama-server single-model and router profiles. Record the exact tested versions during implementation rather than declaring every release compatible. An exported Unsloth model served by llama.cpp uses the llama.cpp adapter, not a separate imagined protocol.

## Public inference contracts

**API-01 — C.** Support text, image, audio, structured decisions, and extension to new inference protocols. Embeddings are included because they appear in the scheduling examples. Scope authorization by actual operation and payload, not only by URL or model alias.

**API-02 — P, Q10.** The first compatibility contract should include model listing, chat completions with streaming and client-executed tool calls, embeddings, image generation, audio transcription, speech generation, and one named structured-decision API. Expose only features supported by the chosen deployment. Full Responses, Messages, video, realtime duplex audio, and other contracts are additional explicit coverage decisions, not implied by the phrase OpenAI-compatible.

**API-03 — I.** Preserve supported request parameters, response semantics, structured output, usage accounting, cancellation, and streaming error behavior. Reject an unsupported parameter or endpoint clearly when dropping it would change meaning. Do not pretend that a plain chat response implements a structured-decision protocol.

**API-04 — I.** An adapter declares whether a request is synchronous, streamed, or a job with later result retrieval; what state or file handles it creates; and how cancellation and cleanup work. Provider-local IDs are namespaced and routed back to their owner. A server-held conversation or media handle cannot move to another endpoint unless the required state is transferable.

**API-05 — P, Q11.** Permit model-generated tool calls that the client executes, but disable provider-side code execution, web tools, and MCP execution through Mango by default. A localhost backend may otherwise interpret a proxied request as locally trusted. Any future server-side tool permission must be separate from inference permission and reviewed at the owning node.

## Catalog and aliases

**MODEL-01 — C.** Detect hosted models from their endpoints. Allow the user to assign an alias, capability labels, and a rating for each label. A request using an alias is served by an eligible deployment registered under that alias. Translate the alias to the provider's real identifier at the boundary.

**MODEL-02 — C.** The same alias may represent different quantizations, formats, machines, or even unrelated models of different quality. Validate that deployments sharing it accept the same input modalities and produce the same output modalities. Do not validate honesty of names or ratings, model intelligence, or equivalence of weights.

**MODEL-03 — I.** Retain each deployment's real provider identity, artifact identity where available, loaded-instance identity, actual context limit, technical features, performance, and memory profile. An alias is a grouping label, not a reason to average away hard limits or copy another instance's cache claim.

**MODEL-04 — I.** Separate user task ratings from protocol support. A model rated highly for coding is not thereby proven to support tools, structured JSON, image input, or a particular decision schema. Request-specific features must be matched against the deployment's actual support.

**MODEL-05 — P, Q12/Q28.** Use shared capability labels with deployment-specific integer ratings from 0 to 5; leave unrated distinct from 0. Allow bulk assignment to an alias, with individual overrides. Enforce exact input/output modality sets for shared aliases initially. Broader subset matching is a later policy choice.

**MODEL-06 — P, Q12.** Add a technical output-contract check for embeddings, such as vector dimensions and encoding. This is an explicit extension to the user's modality-only validation rule. Even equal-length embeddings from different models need not share a meaningful vector space: warn about mixing them, and pin an embedding collection to an explicit deployment or owner-declared compatible family. Do not claim to verify semantic equivalence.

**MODEL-07 — I.** Alias changes are revisioned and conflict-checked. An in-flight request retains its resolved deployment and original alias revision. Renaming a model cannot retarget a request midstream. When another node is offline, the UI shows that the change is pending there.

**MODEL-08 — I.** Distinguish discoverable, eligible, and immediately available models in listing and UI. A busy model remains in the catalog; a leech advertises no executable capacity. Inaccessible or unverified context information must not be represented as an unlimited context.

## Served context and input fit

**CONTEXT-01 — C.** Detect the maximum context actually served by a configured instance, not only the model's theoretical training limit. Store theoretical and effective limits separately when both are known. Recheck effective limits after reloads and server configuration changes.

**CONTEXT-02 — I.** For generation, fit the encoded prompt, template and system overhead, tool definitions, multimodal tokens, and reserved output into the effective context. Count with the destination's tokenizer or an authoritative provider count when available. Different deployments under one alias may tokenize the same input differently.

**CONTEXT-03 — I.** Do not fill the entire context with input and then expect output to fit. A full-context benchmark means total input plus its reserved output reaches the usable limit. For embedding and media endpoints, use the appropriate input, batch, duration, resolution, or output limits rather than forcing a text context concept onto them.

**CONTEXT-04 — P, Q13.** If an adapter cannot discover a reliable effective limit, require a user-supplied served limit or a bounded verification procedure before advertising that capacity. Mark its provenance as reported, measured, or user-configured. Token estimates must be conservative, and the serving node retains final validation. Never silently truncate a request to make it fit.

## Benchmarking and resource profiles

**BENCH-01 — C.** Measure short, approximately half-context, and full-served-context requests for text-like models where those tests make sense. Measure system resource use during model loading and execution so the scheduler can judge safe overlap. Do not apply these three prompt lengths indiscriminately to image or audio endpoints.

**BENCH-02 — I.** Record load time, prompt processing time or rate where exposed, time to first token, generation rate, completion time, peak RAM, peak VRAM per device, and configuration. Distinguish cold loading, warm execution, and actual cache reuse. Record unsupported or unobserved metrics as unknown, never zero.

**BENCH-03 — I.** A model's resource cost includes weights, context/KV cache, concurrency, temporary buffers, media encoders or projectors, runtime overhead, and transient load peaks. Record the request size and simultaneous work used for each measurement. One isolated load is insufficient evidence that two models at full context can safely overlap.

**BENCH-04 — P, Q13.** Benchmark with synthetic inputs, opt-in permission, visible progress, cancellation, and a time/resource budget. Run low-cost discovery first, then short, middle, and full tests subject to safety. If a test is skipped or cannot safely finish, retain an explicit incomplete profile and schedule conservatively. Do not silently replace the requested full-context measurement with a tiny sample.

**BENCH-05 — I.** Bind measurements to the artifact, quantization, runtime version, device configuration, context size, cache configuration, concurrency, and relevant adapter version. Material changes invalidate affected confidence. Rebenchmark on relevant changes or user request, not every startup.

**BENCH-06 — P, Q14.** Allow overlapping deployments only with adequate resource evidence and a current admission check. Use conservative non-overlap for unmeasured combinations; permit a local owner to configure a qualified profile. Do not benchmark every possible combination combinatorially, and do not extrapolate a small-context peak into a claim of full-context safety.

## Required catalog information

This is a logical information contract, not a storage schema.

| Record | Required information |
| --- | --- |
| Provider endpoint | Owner node, adapter and version, endpoint, credential reference, management authority, health, available operations |
| Deployment | Provider model ID, alias, artifact/variant where known, modalities, supported tasks/features, limits, installation/load state |
| Loaded instance | Instance ID, runtime/configuration fingerprint, effective context, devices, slots/concurrency, observed memory, cache/state support |
| Capability assessment | Label, per-deployment rating, editor, revision; explicit missing rating |
| Benchmark | Workload dimensions, cold/warm/cache condition, timings, memory peaks, confidence/provenance, environment, timestamp |
| Availability | Contributor state, accepting/busy/withdrawn, bounded capacity hint, observation revision and freshness |

### Research implications

LM Studio distinguishes loaded-instance context configuration from the model maximum and provides a native management API. llama-server's supported mode and version determine management and event facilities. Unsloth documents an API, including multimodal and decision routes, whose availability depends on version, backend, and model. These are reasons to probe capability rather than infer it from a provider's name. See the source summaries in [Research](07-research-and-recommendations.md).
